responsibility.value: Orchestrates the write side of the rental lifecycle: creates rental requests and drives every store/student-initiated state transition through IRentalStateMachine, wrapping each operation in a DB transaction and dispatching notifications.

Owns: Transaction boundary for every command (ExecuteInTransactionAsync wraps create + all transitions)
Actor-scoped loading — LoadForStoreAsync / LoadForStudentAsync enforce that the caller may only touch rentals belonging to their store or their own student profile
Instrument-lock conflict pre-check before Approve/Pickup, passed into the state machine via RentalTransitionContext
Translating the unique-constraint violation (UX_InstrumentRental_InstrumentId_ActiveOrApproved) into a BusinessException with a user-facing message
Post-transition notification dispatch and the second SaveChangesAsync that persists the resulting outbox row
doesNotOwn: Transition legality — delegated entirely to IRentalStateMachine.Fire
Actor identity resolution — ICurrentActor is trusted as already-authenticated
Notification delivery — only dispatches; IRentalNotificationDispatcher owns the outbox/publish mechanics

collaborators.detail: Fire() is the sole transition authority; result is trusted as-is
Resolves current student profile / store id for scoping
Fire-and-forget-style dispatch after each successful mutation, same transaction
Static ApplyBilling call when building the returned DTO
Owns the transaction and SaveChangesAsync calls
Loads, mutates via state machine, and persists this aggregate

contracts: Every public method runs inside a single DB transaction; on any exception the transaction is rolled back and the exception rethrown.
A student can only Cancel their own rental (LoadForStudentAsync throws BusinessException on mismatch); a store employee can only act on rentals belonging to their own store (LoadForStoreAsync).

If the state machine returns a failure result, the transaction still contains only the failed read — no partial mutation is persisted (BusinessException thrown before any SaveChangesAsync for that path).

The unique constraint on (InstrumentId, Active/Approved) is the actual source of truth for 'one active rental per instrument' — the AnyAsync pre-check in ExecuteTransitionAsync is a UX optimization, not the enforcement mechanism.
assumptions: The instrument-lock AnyAsync pre-check and the later unique-constraint save happen in the same transaction, so a genuine race is still caught — but there is a TOCTOU window between the check and the guard evaluation inside Fire().

SaveWithLockConflictMessageAsync's DbUpdateException matching is done by substring on InnerException.Message against the literal index name 'UX_InstrumentRental_InstrumentId_ActiveOrApproved' — this is provider-specific (works for the current EF provider's exception text) and would silently stop working if the DB provider or index name changes.

rental.Instrument and rental.Instrument.InstrumentType are assumed already loaded (via WithRentalDetails()) before ExecuteTransitionAsync reads rental.Instrument.InstrumentType.MonthlyFee — an unloaded navigation would NRE, not fail gracefully.
actor.UserId is trusted as the authenticated caller's id with no re-verification against the loaded rental's owner beyond the AppUserId/MusicStoreId comparisons already made.
invariants: Every code path either commits a fully-applied transition or rolls back and rethrows — there is no path that returns a DTO reflecting a state that wasn't actually persisted.
CreatedById / actor.UserId is stamped on new rentals at creation time; audit fields on transitions are stamped by the state machine, not this class.
failureModes: MembershipInactive — student's membership isn't active at request time (BusinessException)
InstrumentNotFound — target instrument doesn't exist or isn't active (NotFoundException)
RentalPendingRequired — student already has a pending request for this instrument (BusinessException)
RentalAccessDenied — actor doesn't own/manage the rental being acted on (BusinessException)
InstrumentReservedOrRented — unique constraint violation surfaced as a friendly message (BusinessException)
Any state-machine Fire() failure — e.g. invalid transition for current status (BusinessException wrapping result.Error)
architecturalNotes: Two SaveChangesAsync calls per transition (one inside ExecuteTransitionAsync, one in ExecuteTransitionWithNotificationAsync for the outbox row) — both inside the same transaction, so this is a modeling choice, not a correctness gap.

LoadDtoAsync has two overloads (by entity, by id) with a comment noting the entity overload requires the caller to have loaded navigation properties via WithRentalDetails() — an implicit precondition not enforced by the type system.
